challenges.name: find-the-first-bottleneck-evidence
challenges.title: Find the First Bottleneck: read the evidence
challenges.description: The weekly report said POST /api/submissions averages 120 ms; learners in the exam rehearsal waited up to 6 seconds at the deadline while API CPU sat at 40%. Six statements on one evidence pack - the k6 summary (A), the traces (B) and the metrics (C) - take you from reading the evidence to a hypothesis, past a wrong explanation, to the mechanism, the fix and its verification.

questions.question:
Evidence A - k6 end-of-test summary, exam rehearsal on staging (2 API instances). Profile: 160 submissions/s for 2 hours with a deadline spike of 340/s for 80 s at 1h55m (the exam-day forecast).

  http_req_duration..: avg=120.4ms min=6.2ms med=41.3ms max=6.14s p(90)=58.9ms p(95)=74.0ms p(99)=3.64s
  http_req_failed....: 0.00%  0 out of 1,166,412
  http_reqs..........: 1,166,412  161.8/s

The weekly report took one line from this run: "POST /api/submissions: average 120 ms".

Statement: "The 120 ms average and the 6 s waits do not contradict each other: p(99) is 3.64 s, so more than 11,000 requests took longer than 3.6 s, and they are only about 1% of a run that was calm for almost two hours."
questions.explanation: True. 1% of 1,166,412 requests is about 11,700 requests at or above 3.64 s, up to the 6.14 s maximum. Even at 3.6 s each they add at least 11,700 x 3.6 s / 1,166,412 = about 36 ms to the average, and the rest of the slow spike requests add more; the other 98% at about 41 ms make up the rest of the 120 ms. The misconception is that an average close to normal means nobody had a bad time: an average spreads a short, severe incident over hours of quiet traffic.

questions.question:
Evidence A - k6 end-of-test summary, exam rehearsal on staging (2 API instances). Profile: 160 submissions/s for 2 hours with a deadline spike of 340/s for 80 s at 1h55m (the exam-day forecast).

  http_req_duration..: avg=120.4ms min=6.2ms med=41.3ms max=6.14s p(90)=58.9ms p(95)=74.0ms p(99)=3.64s
  http_req_failed....: 0.00%  0 out of 1,166,412
  http_reqs..........: 1,166,412  161.8/s

The weekly report took one line from this run: "POST /api/submissions: average 120 ms".

Statement: "p(95)=74.0ms shows that at least 95% of the submissions sent during the deadline spike got a response within 74 ms."
questions.explanation: False. The percentiles in A are computed over the whole two-hour run. The 80 s spike plus the time to drain its queue is only about 2-3% of all requests, so the whole-run p95 is decided by the calm part and says nothing about the spike. Split the run by time (or tag the spike as its own scenario) and compute the percentiles of the spike alone; B shows its p95 at 5.83 s. The misconception is that a percentile describes every period of the run; it describes the population it was computed on.

questions.question:
Evidence B - traces of POST /api/submissions (server side), p50 / p95 per span:

span                              at 160/s          deadline spike
POST /api/submissions             41 ms / 68 ms     3.05 s / 5.83 s
  auth + validate                  2 ms /  4 ms      2 ms /  4 ms
  db.pool.acquire                  0 ms /  1 ms     3.01 s / 5.79 s
  tx: INSERT submissions           4 ms /  9 ms      5 ms / 11 ms
  tx: PUT source to storage       27 ms / 44 ms     28 ms / 46 ms
  tx: enqueue judge job            1 ms /  2 ms      1 ms /  3 ms
  tx: COMMIT                       2 ms /  4 ms      2 ms /  5 ms

Evidence C - metrics:
                                  at 160/s          deadline spike
submissions accepted per second   160               316
API CPU (2 instances, average)    21%               40%
DB pool per instance (max 6)      3.0 in use        6 in use all the time
requests waiting for the pool     0                 grows to 1,920
mean connection hold time         38 ms             38 ms
PostgreSQL CPU                    15%               31%

Statement: "In the spike, almost all of the 5.83 s p95 is time spent waiting in db.pool.acquire, which is also why API CPU can stay at 40%: a request that waits for a connection uses almost no CPU."
questions.explanation: True. Every span except db.pool.acquire stays within a few milliseconds of its value at 160/s; the acquire wait goes from 1 ms to 5.79 s at p95. A request waiting in the pool's queue holds memory and a slot, but no CPU, so the CPU graph cannot show this kind of saturation. The misconception is "CPU at 40% means there is headroom": CPU is one resource of many, and the first one to saturate here is the connection pool.

Evidence B - traces of POST /api/submissions (server side), p50 / p95 per span:

POST /api/submissions             41 ms / 68 ms     3.05 s / 5.83 s
  auth + validate                  2 ms /  4 ms      2 ms /  4 ms
  db.pool.acquire                  0 ms /  1 ms     3.01 s / 5.79 s
  tx: INSERT submissions           4 ms /  9 ms      5 ms / 11 ms
  tx: PUT source to storage       27 ms / 44 ms     28 ms / 46 ms
  tx: enqueue judge job            1 ms /  2 ms      1 ms /  3 ms
  tx: COMMIT                       2 ms /  4 ms      2 ms /  5 ms

Evidence C - metrics:
                                  at 160/s          deadline spike
submissions accepted per second   160               316
API CPU (2 instances, average)    21%               40%
DB pool per instance (max 6)      3.0 in use        6 in use all the time
requests waiting for the pool     0                 grows to 1,920
mean connection hold time         38 ms             38 ms
PostgreSQL CPU                    15%               31%

Statement: "The database is the first bottleneck: under load each INSERT got slower, the connections stayed busy longer, and the pool ran out. Tuning the INSERT (an index, a faster disk) is the fix."
questions.explanation: False. The INSERT is 5 ms at p50 and 11 ms at p95 in the spike, almost the same as at 160/s, and PostgreSQL CPU is at 31%. The mean hold time of a connection is 38 ms both at 160/s and in the spike, and most of it is the PUT of the source code to object storage, which runs inside the transaction while the connection is held. The database is not slow; the connection is held for work that does not need it. The misconception is that a pool running out means the database is slow.

questions.question:
Evidence B - traces of POST /api/submissions (server side), p50 / p95 per span:

span                              at 160/s          deadline spike
POST /api/submissions             41 ms / 68 ms     3.05 s / 5.83 s
  auth + validate                  2 ms /  4 ms      2 ms /  4 ms
  db.pool.acquire                  0 ms /  1 ms     3.01 s / 5.79 s
  tx: INSERT submissions           4 ms /  9 ms      5 ms / 11 ms
  tx: PUT source to storage       27 ms / 44 ms     28 ms / 46 ms
  tx: enqueue judge job            1 ms /  2 ms      1 ms /  3 ms
  tx: COMMIT                       2 ms /  4 ms      2 ms /  5 ms

Evidence C - metrics:
                                  at 160/s          deadline spike
submissions accepted per second   160               316
API CPU (2 instances, average)    21%               40%
DB pool per instance (max 6)      3.0 in use        6 in use all the time
requests waiting for the pool     0                 grows to 1,920
mean connection hold time         38 ms             38 ms
PostgreSQL CPU                    15%               31%

Statement: "With 12 connections in total, each held for 38 ms on average, the API can accept at most about 316 submissions per second, so at 340/s the queue for the pool must grow for as long as the spike lasts."
questions.explanation: True. By Little's Law, connections in use = throughput x hold time, so the most the pool can serve is 12 / 0.038 s = about 316 submissions per second, which is what C measured during the spike. At 340/s, about 24 more requests arrive every second than the pool can serve, and over 80 s that is the 1,920 waiting requests in C: each new request waits behind all of them, about 1,920 / 316 = 6 s. The misconception is to look for a slow component; at full utilisation the wait comes from the arrival rate exceeding the service rate, even when every step is fast.

questions.question:
The team moves the PUT to object storage out of the transaction (it runs before BEGIN; the row stores the object key), so a connection is held for about 10 ms instead of 38 ms.

Statement: "To verify the fix, rerun the same exam rehearsal: if the average of POST /api/submissions in the k6 summary drops below 120 ms, the bottleneck is gone."
questions.explanation: False. The average was the number that hid the incident in the first place: the rerun could show a lower average while the spike still queues (for example if the PUT got faster for other reasons). Verify the mechanism and the user-visible symptom instead: the p95 and max of the spike period alone, db.pool.acquire in the traces, the waiting requests and the hold time in the pool metrics (about 10 ms), and a step test that shows where the next knee is now. The misconception is that the metric that failed to show the problem can prove it is fixed.

challenges.name: fix-the-bottleneck-finder
challenges.title: Find the First Bottleneck
challenges.description:
CodeDev runs a step load test of POST /api/submissions before every exam: the offered rate rises in steps, and for each step a script collects, per resource, its average utilization and the time each request waited for it. tools/perf/bottleneck.py should name the first bottleneck: the resource where requests started to wait first. On the exam-day step test it reported db_pool at 340 req/s, the last step, although the p95 pool wait was already above the limit at 280 req/s, and it also lists judge_workers as saturated, although no submit request ever waits for a judge worker (the judge runs asynchronously). Fix find_first_bottleneck so that it follows the rule below.

Input (stdin, JSON): {"wait_limit_ms": L, "steps": [{"rate": offered req/s, "resources": {"<name>": {"util": 0..1, "waits_ms": [wait samples in ms]}, ...}}, ...]}. Steps can be in any order. A step whose rate is not a number greater than 0 (missing, a string, a bool, 0 or negative) is ignored. A resource can have no "util", and no or an empty "waits_ms" (no request waited for it).

Rule:
- A resource is saturated at a step when the p95 of its waits_ms at that step is greater than L. Utilization is not part of the rule: a resource can be busy all the time without making requests wait, and an average utilization hides waits.
- Its from_rate is the lowest rate at which it is saturated, even if it is not saturated at some higher step.
- "saturated" lists every saturated resource as {"resource", "from_rate", "p95_wait_ms"} (p95_wait_ms = the p95 wait at from_rate, rounded with round(v, 1)), sorted by from_rate, then by the higher p95 wait (unrounded), then by name.
- first_bottleneck and at_rate are the resource and from_rate of the first entry, or null and null when nothing is saturated.

Percentiles: nearest-rank on sorted samples, rank = ceil(p/100 * n), value = sorted[rank - 1]; an empty list has no percentile (the starter's percentile function already does this).

Output: {"first_bottleneck": name or null, "at_rate": rate or null, "saturated": [...]}. Example: {"first_bottleneck": "db_pool", "at_rate": 280, "saturated": [{"resource": "db_pool", "from_rate": 280, "p95_wait_ms": 140}]}.
hints: Run the starter on the first public test and compare two things with the rule: which resources does it call saturated, and at which rate does it say each one started? For each, ask what evidence it used - a wait, or something else.

Look at the condition that marks a resource as saturated and at the line that stores the result: what happens to the stored from_rate when the same resource is saturated again at a later step? Then check the sort key for two resources that saturate at the same step.

A similar case with other data: steps 100, 200, 300; the cache shows util 0.95, 0.97, 0.99 and wait p95 2, 3, 4 ms; the disk queue shows util 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and wait p95 10, 80, 300 ms; limit 50 ms. Only the disk queue makes requests wait above the limit, first at 200, so the report is disk queue from 200 with p95 80 - not 300, where it is still saturated.

tests.name: Exam-day step test: the pool wait crosses the limit first, CPU never does
Small test: a busy resource with short waits is not saturated
Two resources saturate at the same step: the higher p95 wait comes first
Waits only in the tail: the p95 is over the limit while the mean is not
Steps out of order, a resource that recovers for one step keeps its first rate
Nothing waits above the limit: no bottleneck in the tested range
Invalid steps are ignored; missing waits or util are handled
Large step test: 30 steps, 6 resources, 60 wait samples each
